pairs.rationale: Both introduce Paul as Christ Jesus' apostle through God's will and address saints. Corinthians names Timothy and its Corinth/Achaia recipients; Ephesians has no named co-sender and preserves the original brackets around in Ephesus.
Both give grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. This is a shared greeting formula addressed to different communities, not an additional event.

Both bless the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Ephesians names every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ; Peter's letter names merciful new birth and living hope through Jesus' resurrection.

Both connect divine purpose in Christ with a holy calling or life and a time before the present ages. Ephesians says chosen before the world's foundation; Timothy's letter names purpose and grace before the ages. The temporal expressions remain distinct.

Both relate adoption as sons to God's action through Jesus Christ. Galatians describes sending and redeeming through the Son and then the Spirit's cry; Ephesians emphasizes predestination according to God's good pleasure rather than repeating that sequence.

The praise-of-His-glory refrain recurs after the inheritance and prior-hope statements. Here it specifically names the glory of His grace and favor in the Beloved. This is an internal doxological pattern, not an identical additional benefit.

Both join redemption with forgiveness. Ephesians says transgressions, through His blood and according to grace's riches; the actual Colossians unit says sins and does not include an added through-His-blood clause.

Ephesians describes grace lavished in wisdom and understanding; Colossians prays for knowledge of God's will in spiritual wisdom and understanding. The related intellectual vocabulary belongs to a declaration in one and a petition in the other.

Both describe a divine mystery made known to believers. Ephesians names God's will and good pleasure; Colossians describes prior hiding, present disclosure and Christ in you as hope of glory. Their stated content and emphasis remain distinct.

Both place all things in the heavens and on earth in relation to Christ. Ephesians speaks of summing them up in Him at the fullness of times; Colossians speaks of reconciliation and peace through the cross's blood. The actions are not made identical.

Both describe an inheritance connected with divine provision. Ephesians names being allotted an inheritance according to predestining purpose; Colossians thanks the Father for enabling a share in the saints' inheritance in light. The formulations differ.

Praise of His glory repeats the earlier refrain about the glory of His grace. Here it follows we who hoped beforehand in Christ. The comparison preserves the additional prior-hope wording without assigning the we group an unprinted ethnic identity.

Both describe divine sealing and the Spirit. Corinthians also names establishing, anointing and the Spirit's pledge in hearts; Ephesians names hearing the gospel, believing and the promised Holy Spirit. Their recipients and expressed sequence remain distinct.

Both name the Spirit as a pledge. Ephesians relates the pledge to inheritance and redemption of the possession; Corinthians relates it to God's preparing the speakers in the bodily-life argument. The accompanying images and objects are preserved.

Both report hearing of the readers' faith in Jesus and love toward all the saints. Ephesians names the Lord Jesus while Colossians names Christ Jesus; the correspondence does not identify their readerships as one congregation.

Both join thanksgiving for the readers with continuing prayer. Ephesians uses the writer's first-person singular remembrance; Colossians describes we giving thanks and praying. The letter situations and pronouns remain distinct.

Both prayers seek divinely given understanding. Ephesians asks the God of the Lord Jesus Christ, Father of glory, for a spirit of wisdom and revelation in knowing Him; Colossians asks for knowledge of His will in spiritual wisdom and understanding.

Both connect divine inheritance and hoped-for glory. Ephesians asks that the heart know the calling's hope and His inheritance's glory among the saints; Romans calls God's children heirs with Christ and anticipates revealed glory. The possessive wording and Romans’s suffering qualification remain distinct.

The later doxology again names power working in us. Here the prayer concerns the surpassing greatness of God's power toward believers; later God's ability exceeds asking or thinking. This is a recurring internal power theme rather than a second miracle report.

Both describe Christ raised from the dead and at God's right hand. Ephesians explicitly describes God exercising power and seating Him in heavenly places; Romans also names His death and intercession for us. Their additional claims remain distinct.

Both describe Christ's exaltation above every name. Philippians develops universal bending of knees and confession to God the Father's glory; Ephesians lists rule, authority, power and dominion across this age and the coming one. The lists and formulations differ.

The all-things-under-His-feet clause corresponds to the Psalm's subjection formula. Ephesians applies it to Christ and adds His headship for the Church; that Church clause is not supplied as part of the Psalm's creation-language setting.

Both explicitly call the Church Christ's body. Colossians names Him as its head and firstborn from the dead; Ephesians describes its fullness relation to the One who fills all things. The additional fullness wording is not silently inserted into the selected Colossians unit.

Both describe the recipients as dead in transgressions. Colossians also names uncircumcision and being made alive with forgiveness; the Ephesians sentence develops its own former-life description before reaching made-alive language in2:5.

Both describe hostile power associated with the age and disobedience or unbelief. Ephesians names the ruler of the air's authority and a working spirit; Corinthians names the god of this age blinding minds. The titles and actions are not treated as one verbatim formula.

Both look back on a former life directed by desires. Titus also lists deception, malice, envy and hatred; Ephesians speaks of flesh and thought and children of wrath by nature. The lists and the nature statement are not made identical.

Both locate salvation in divine mercy and love rather than the recipients' prior worthiness. Titus names God's kindness and love for humanity and saving mercy; Ephesians names God's abundant mercy and great love before its made-alive statement.

Both speak of people dead in transgressions being made alive together with Christ. Ephesians explicitly adds by grace you have been saved; Colossians also describes forgiving all transgressions. The additional clauses stay in their own passages.

Both refer to being raised together with Christ. Ephesians also says seated together in heavenly places in Christ; Colossians commands seeking what is above where Christ is seated at God's right hand. It does not explicitly say the readers are seated there in that unit.

The riches-of-His-grace wording recurs. Earlier it describes redemption through Christ's blood and forgiveness; here the future ages display surpassing grace's riches in kindness in Christ. The present benefit and future display remain distinct.

Both attribute salvation or justification to divine grace. Romans names being justified freely by His grace through redemption in Christ; Ephesians says saved by grace through faith and adds that this is not from yourselves but God's gift. The terms justification and salvation remain distinct.

Both exclude boasting in an argument about works and faith. Ephesians says not from works so no one boasts; Romans asks where boasting is and contrasts a law of works with a law of faith. The different law wording is preserved.

Both describe a divinely formed or redeemed people directed toward good works. Titus names Christ's self-giving to purify a people zealous for them; Ephesians names God's workmanship and prior preparation of the works to walk in. The actions differ.

Both discuss circumcision and flesh or hands. Ephesians recalls Gentile labels and circumcision made by hands in flesh; Colossians describes circumcision not made by hands in Christ. The physical description and Christ-centered metaphor remain distinct.

Israel, covenants and promise are explicitly connected in both. Romans lists Israelite privileges; Ephesians recalls Gentile alienation from Israel's commonwealth and promise covenants before the following nearness statement.

Both relate access or nearness to Jesus' blood. Ephesians describes formerly distant recipients made near by Christ's blood; Hebrews describes confidence to enter the holy places by Jesus' blood. The spatial images and addressed circumstances remain distinct.

Christ as our peace and the breaking of hostility correspond to making peace through the cross's blood in the reconciliation account. Ephesians focuses on both groups becoming one; Colossians names things on earth and in heaven. The scopes differ.

Both describe the removal of a barrier expressed through decrees. Ephesians names abolishing the law of commandments in decrees to create one new human being; Colossians names a hostile handwritten record removed at the cross. The law and record descriptions are not simply equated.

Both join reconciliation with Christ's bodily death. Ephesians says both are reconciled in one body to God through the cross; Colossians says in His fleshly body through death, with holy presentation as its aim. The body formulations are kept distinct.

The peace-to-far-and-near wording corresponds to Isaiah's peace saying. Ephesians presents Christ proclaiming it to the readers and those near; Isaiah's actual saying has its own Lord/healing context. The source is a scriptural echo rather than a supplied identical narrative event.

Both describe access through Jesus Christ. Ephesians explicitly says both have access in one Spirit to the Father; Romans joins access by faith into grace with peace toward God through the Lord Jesus Christ. The Spirit and faith formulations are not substituted for each other.

Both describe a community as a household. Ephesians contrasts foreigner status with being fellow citizens and God's household; Galatians gives the household of faith particular attention in doing good. The images and immediate purposes remain distinct.

The cornerstone image corresponds to Isaiah's chosen, precious cornerstone laid in Zion's foundations. Ephesians names Christ Jesus as cornerstone within its apostles-and-prophets foundation image; Isaiah's actual trust-in-it wording and setting are preserved rather than silently rewritten as the whole Ephesians sentence.

Both picture believers being built into a holy community. Ephesians describes the fitted building growing into a holy sanctuary; Peter's letter describes living stones and a spiritual house with priesthood and sacrifices. The added priestly details are not inserted into Ephesians.

Both describe the community as God's dwelling through the Spirit. Corinthians calls the readers God's temple with the Spirit dwelling among them; Ephesians describes their being built together into God's dwelling in the Spirit. The construction emphasis is specific here.
Both explicitly call Paul a prisoner of Christ Jesus. Ephesians adds for you Gentiles; Philemon names Timothy and its recipient. The shared designation does not identify a prison location or date.

Both describe a stewardship from God given to the speaker for the recipients. Ephesians names the stewardship of grace; Colossians names service and fulfilling God's word. The related commission language is not one identical description of every task.

Both ground Paul's received message in revelation rather than merely human instruction. Ephesians names the mystery made known by revelation; Galatians names the gospel and revelation of Jesus Christ. No particular vision or prior writing is identified by this comparison.

The later that-clause gives the expressed mystery's content: Gentile fellow heirs, body members and promise sharers in Christ through the gospel. This supplies concrete internal content for what the readers can perceive by reading, without identifying an unpreserved earlier document.

Both contrast earlier concealment with present disclosure of a mystery. Romans names prophetic writings and all nations; Ephesians names holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit and says not made known as now. Their temporal qualifications and means of disclosure remain distinct.

Both connect unity in Christ across Jew/Greek distinctions with inheritance and promise. Galatians names Abraham's seed and heirs according to promise; Ephesians names Gentile fellow heirs, body membership and sharing through the gospel. The additional categories remain in their own passages.

Both attribute Paul's ministry to God's given grace and working. Corinthians describes labor with God's grace rather than himself alone; Ephesians calls him a servant by grace's gift and divine power. The roles and personal expressions differ.

Both combine Paul's ministry with a least designation. Corinthians calls him least of the apostles and mentions persecuting God's Church; Ephesians calls him least of all saints and commissioned to proclaim Christ's riches to the nations. Neither comparison substitutes apostles for saints.

Both speak of a mystery hidden through ages and now made known. Colossians locates its riches among the nations and identifies Christ in you as hope of glory; Ephesians names its administration and God as creator. Their descriptions are not merged.

Both connect revealed salvation with heavenly observers. Peter says angels desire to look into the proclaimed things; Ephesians says God's varied wisdom is made known through the Church to heavenly rulers and authorities. Angels and those authorities are not assigned identical activities or identities.

Both locate divine purpose in Christ with an ages-related horizon. Ephesians says the purpose of the ages accomplished in Christ Jesus; Timothy's letter names purpose and grace given before the times of the ages. The temporal and ministry statements differ.

Both describe access through Christ associated with faith. Romans names peace toward God and access into grace; Ephesians names boldness and confident access in Him. Their benefits and actual formulations remain distinct.

Both place ministry suffering or weakness within benefit for the recipients and refuse discouragement. Corinthians joins for-your-sake language with not losing heart and inner renewal; Ephesians asks the readers not to lose heart at afflictions called their glory. The persons addressed differ.

Both describe Paul kneeling to pray. Acts narrates kneeling with the assembled companions; Ephesians directs his bowed knees before the Father and continues with the petition. The posture corresponds without identifying the occasions or participants.

The Father before whom Paul bends his knees supplies the antecedent of from whom in the following statement about every family being named. This identifies the stated referent without independently repeating the family-naming assertion or assigning an unprinted angelic or genealogical identity to the heavenly and earthly families.

Both distinguish the inner person as the site of divine renewal or strengthening. Corinthians speaks of daily renewal amid outward wasting; Ephesians prays for strengthening through the Father's Spirit according to His glory. The actions and surrounding contrast differ.

Christ dwelling through faith in hearts corresponds to Christ in you as hope of glory. Colossians also places the mystery's riches among the nations; Ephesians adds being rooted and founded in love. The spatial and accompanying metaphors remain distinct.

The following clause joins knowing Christ's knowledge-surpassing love and fullness of God to the prayer about grasping breadth, length, height and depth. This gives the dimensions their immediate prayer context without assigning a measured physical object to them.

Both connect the recipients' fullness with Christ and divine fullness. Colossians says deity's fullness dwells bodily in Him and the readers are filled in Him; Ephesians prays for fullness while knowing Christ's surpassing love. The subjects of those different fullness statements remain distinct.

Both describe God's ability in terms of abundance toward believers. Corinthians connects abounding grace with sufficiency and good works; Ephesians says His working power exceeds asking or thinking. The collection context and doxological setting remain distinct.

Both conclude with glory to God through the ages and Amen. Ephesians explicitly names the Church, Christ Jesus and every generation; Romans precedes its doxology with all things from, through and to Him. The praise formulas correspond without being identical.

Both urge a worthy walk. Ephesians relates it to the calling with which the readers were called; Colossians relates it to the Lord, pleasing Him, fruitful work and growing knowledge. The object of worthy and the additional aims remain distinct.

Both list humility, gentleness, patience and bearing with one another in a loving community. Colossians also explicitly names forgiveness and love as a bond; Ephesians places these qualities within its unity exhortation. Their lists are not made identical.

Both join a communal bond with peace and unity. Ephesians names unity of the Spirit in peace's bond; Colossians calls love completeness's bond and names Christ's peace with one-body calling. The differing bonds and divine titles remain as printed.

Both explicitly join one body with one Spirit. Corinthians describes baptism and drinking one Spirit across Jew/Greek and slave/free distinctions; Ephesians adds one hope of calling. Those additional formulations are not exchanged.

Faith and baptism in Christ join believers as one in Galatians. That corresponds to the one-faith/one-baptism statement under one Lord here, while Galatians also names sons of God, clothing in Christ and social distinctions rather than the same three-part list.

Both confess one God, the Father, in relation to all things. Ephesians says over, through and in all; Corinthians says from the Father and for Him, then through the Lord Jesus Christ. The prepositions and Father/Son relations are not silently reassigned.

Both connect received grace with gifts distributed among believers. Ephesians names each person's measure of Christ's gift; Romans names differing gifts according to given grace. Its prophecy/faith wording does not replace Christ's-gift wording here.

The ascended-on-high and captivity-captive clauses correspond to the Psalm. The decisive difference is preserved: Ephesians says He gave gifts to human beings, whereas the Psalm says Thou received gifts among human beings. This is an adapted scriptural use, not an unchanged reproduction.

Both connect ascent with a descent by the same figure. John names the Son of Man coming down from heaven; Ephesians reasons from He ascended to descent into the lower parts of the earth. John does not resolve that latter location phrase.

Both describe Christ's exaltation above the heavens. Hebrews identifies the fitting high priest and His character; Ephesians identifies the descended and ascended One and His filling all things. Their stated roles and additional actions remain distinct.

Both list apostles, prophets and teachers among divinely provided ministries. Corinthians makes God the appointer and adds powers, healings, helps, guidance and tongues; Ephesians describes Christ giving and adds evangelists and shepherds. Their ordering and lists are preserved.

Both make communal building up a purpose of spiritual provision. Corinthians addresses those zealous for spirits and tells them to excel for the Church's building; Ephesians names equipping saints for service and building Christ's body through the given people. Their actual terms remain distinct.

Both set maturity in Christ as a ministry goal. Colossians speaks of proclaiming and teaching to present every person mature in Christ; Ephesians names communal unity, knowledge of God's Son and the mature person's measure of Christ's fullness. Individual and corporate emphases differ.

Both warn against being carried away by teaching. Ephesians uses childhood, waves and deceptive human schemes; Hebrews warns of varied strange teachings and contrasts grace with food practices. The examples and grounds are not equated.

Both identify Christ as head in relation to His body, the Church. Ephesians describes truthful loving growth into Him; Colossians names headship, beginning and firstborn from the dead. The different predicates remain distinct.

Both describe a body held together through its supporting parts and growing from the head. Ephesians names each part's proper work and building in love; Colossians names joints and ligaments and growth from God. The statements are closely related without having every identical term.

Both describe futility in thought. Romans links futile reasoning and a darkened heart with failing to honor or thank God; Ephesians warns the readers against the Gentile walk in mind's futility, elaborated in its following sentence. The particular accounts remain distinct.

Both describe alienation linked with the mind. Ephesians names darkened understanding, ignorance and hard hearts alienated from God's life; Colossians names prior alienation and hostile minds in evil works. The causes and expressions remain distinct.

Both use handing-over language with impurity and desires. The actors differ: Ephesians says they handed themselves over; Romans says God handed them over. That difference is preserved rather than turning the two sentences into an identical action.

Learning Christ against the former conduct corresponds to receiving Christ Jesus as Lord and walking in Him as taught. Colossians adds rootedness, building and thanksgiving; Ephesians continues with truth and putting off former conduct. The teaching formulations differ.

Truth in Jesus corresponds to Jesus' statement that He is the way, truth and life. Ephesians frames it as the readers' hearing and learning in Him; John adds access to the Father. The source does not require an unreported physical encounter by every reader.

Both describe putting off the old human being. Ephesians connects former conduct with deceitful desires; Colossians connects the old with practices and adds putting on the new, renewed in knowledge. The shared clothing image does not make the full descriptions identical.

Both describe renewal related to the mind. Romans connects renewal with transformation and discerning God's will; Ephesians specifically says renewed in the spirit of your mind. That lower-case formulation is not silently replaced with a different named agent.

Both describe putting on the new human being in relation to God's creation. Colossians names renewal in knowledge according to the Creator's image; Ephesians names righteousness and holiness of truth. The differing qualities remain distinct.

The speak-truth-each-with-neighbor instruction corresponds to Zechariah's truth-speaking command. Ephesians adds membership in one another as its reason; Zechariah continues into rendering peaceful judgment in the gates. Those additional grounds and instructions remain in their own passages.

The be-angry-and-do-not-sin clause corresponds to the actual Greek-numbered Psalm4:5. Ephesians adds the sunset limit on anger; the Psalm continues with heart-and-bed language. Neither continuation is supplied as part of the other's wording.

Both warn against giving hostile spiritual advantage through communal conduct. Corinthians names Satan's designs within forgiveness; Ephesians forbids giving the devil a place in its anger instructions. The conduct and advantage/place images remain distinct.

Both relate labor with one's hands to supporting others. Ephesians tells the thief to stop stealing and work to share with the needy; Paul in Acts recalls hands supplying needs and labor to help the weak. Acts does not identify Paul as a former thief.

Both direct speech toward grace and an appropriate response to hearers. Colossians adds salt seasoning and knowing how to answer each person; Ephesians excludes rotten speech and requires needed building up. The metaphors and directives remain distinct.

Both connect wrongdoing with offense against God's spirit. Ephesians says not to grieve the Holy Spirit of God and names sealing for redemption; Isaiah says they disobeyed and provoked His holy spirit, followed by hostility and fighting. The actions and printed capitalizations remain distinct.

Both command removal of anger, rage, malice and slander. Ephesians also names bitterness and shouting; Colossians also names foul speech from the mouth. The overlapping lists and their different additional items are preserved.

Both command kindness, tender concern and forgiveness patterned on divine forgiveness. Ephesians says God in Christ forgave you; Colossians names the Lord's forgiveness. The different divine formulations and associated virtues remain as printed.

Both relate believers' conduct to God as model. Matthew commands perfection as the heavenly Father is perfect; Ephesians calls beloved children to imitate God, continued as walking in love. The different commands are not made identical.

Both connect Christ's self-offering with God's saving purpose. Hebrews names sanctification through Jesus Christ's body's offering once for all; Ephesians describes His loving self-giving as an offering and sacrifice to God with fragrant aroma. The temporal and aroma details differ.

Both specifically name sexual immorality, impurity and greed among conduct to reject. Colossians uses putting earthly members to death and calls greed idolatry; Ephesians says these things must not even be named among the readers, as is fitting for saints. The instructions and full lists differ.

Both reject harmful speech. Colossians names foul speech and lying alongside anger and slander; Ephesians names foolish talk and coarse joking and sets thanksgiving as the alternative. The categories are related, not identical.

Both warn that specified wrongdoing is incompatible with inheriting God's kingdom, including sexual immorality, idolatry and greed. Ephesians explicitly links greed and idolatry and names Christ and God's kingdom; Corinthians's longer list and wording remain its own.

Both say that because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. Ephesians also warns about empty-word deception; Colossians places the shared wrath clause after its list of earthly practices. Each letter's surrounding warning is preserved.

The ban on becoming their fellow sharers relates to incompatible fellowship between light and darkness and believer and unbeliever. Ephesians's named context concerns disobedient works; Corinthians uses the unequal-yoke and Christ/Beliar contrasts. Their participation language is not an identical rule about every contact.

Both describe believers through light/day rather than darkness/night. Ephesians makes a former-darkness/now-light-in-the-Lord contrast and commands a corresponding walk; Thessalonians names sons of light and day. The temporal and conduct clauses remain distinct.

Both use fruit language for good qualities and explicitly include goodness. Ephesians says fruit of the light with righteousness and truth; Galatians says fruit of the Spirit and lists other qualities. The word light is not replaced with Spirit in Ephesians.

Testing what pleases the Lord corresponds to discerning God's good, pleasing and perfect will through renewed thinking. Romans includes the transformation command; Ephesians places testing within the light-and-fruit instruction. The divine titles and contexts remain distinct.

Both reject works of darkness. Romans contrasts the advanced night with the near day and putting on light's weapons; Ephesians rejects sharing in unfruitful dark works and instead commands exposure. The differing images and actions remain distinct.

The earlier not-even-be-named instruction about immorality, impurity and greed relates to the later shame of speaking about secret deeds. These are internal discourse warnings in one conduct argument, not a complete identification of every unnamed secret deed.

Both join light with deeds being exposed or made visible. John contrasts evildoers avoiding the light with truth-doers coming to it; Ephesians states the exposing effect of light within its commands about works of darkness. The units explain their own arguments rather than duplicating every claim.

The wake-and-rise-from-death saying relates to Isaiah's dead rising and those in tombs being aroused. Ephesians names Christ shining; that is not a full verbatim Isaiah26 quotation. The comparison retains the different forms rather than identifying the whole saying's precise source.

Christ shining upon the awakened person has a related light-call in Isaiah's address to Jerusalem. The subjects, setting and actual wording differ. This is a bounded light-theme comparison, not a claim that Isaiah60:1 contains the complete wake-from-death saying.

Both direct a wise walk. Colossians explicitly names conduct toward outsiders; Ephesians contrasts wise with unwise walking, followed by using opportunity. The stated recipients of conduct and the contrasting term are kept distinct.

Both join conduct with buying up opportunity. Ephesians states that the days are evil; Colossians places the phrase with a wise walk toward outsiders. Neither additional circumstance is silently inserted into the other unit.

Understanding the Lord's will corresponds to discerning God's good, pleasing and perfect will. Ephesians opposes foolishness; Romans names mind renewal and transformation rather than repeating that same imperative.

Both contrast drunkenness with a different communal orientation. Thessalonians uses wakefulness, sobriety and day/night with faith/love armor; Ephesians contrasts wine's excess with being filled in the Spirit. Their alternatives and images are not made identical.

Both name psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, singing from the heart. Ephesians directs speaking to one another and melody to the Lord; Colossians connects singing to indwelling Christ's word, teaching and gratitude to God. The named directions remain distinct.

Both connect comprehensive action with thanks to God through Jesus. Ephesians says always and for all things in the Lord Jesus' name to God the Father; Colossians names word/deed and thanks through Him. The formulations remain as printed.

Both concern submission or humility in community relations. Ephesians says submitting to one another in the fear of Christ; Peter's letter tells younger people to submit to elders and all to clothe themselves in humility toward one another. The addressees and wording are not collapsed.

Both address wives in relation to their husbands and the Lord. Colossians states its submission verb; the Ephesians unit continues the submitting phrase from5:21 without printing a new verb. That original continuation is preserved.

Both describe Christ as the Church's head in relation to the body. Ephesians uses that relation in its husband/wife analogy and calls Him body-Savior; Colossians adds beginning and firstborn from the dead. The analogy and additional titles remain distinct.

The Church/Christ comparison develops the preceding wives-to-husbands instruction and its continued submission language. The source explicitly states in everything here, while the earlier unit says as to the Lord. This is internal explanation, not a second household episode.

Both tell husbands to love their wives. Ephesians models the love on Christ giving Himself for the Church; Colossians adds not becoming bitter toward wives. The source's Christ/Church example is not supplied as a Colossians clause.

Both use washing language in salvation and purification. Titus names washing of regeneration and Holy Spirit renewal according to mercy; Ephesians names Christ cleansing the Church with water's washing and a word. The stated agents and descriptive elements remain distinct.

Both describe holy, unblemished presentation. Ephesians names Christ presenting the Church glorious without spot or wrinkle; Colossians names reconciliation through His fleshly body and death to present the readers holy and beyond accusation. The images and recipients remain distinct.

Loving one's wife as one's own body relates to the following one-flesh citation about husband and wife. This identifies an explicit internal basis for the shared-body argument without changing the two people into an undifferentiated individual.

Christ's nourishing and cherishing the Church relates to the nursing-mother analogy of cherishing children in apostolic care. Thessalonians additionally describes sharing gospel and lives with beloved readers; the bodily and family images concern different relationships.

Both explicitly describe believers as members of Christ's body. Corinthians addresses the community as His body and individually members; Ephesians gives membership as the reason within the nurturing/Church argument. Its short body wording is preserved without added flesh-and-bones text.

Ephesians cites leaving father and mother, joining the wife and the two becoming one flesh. Genesis supplies that marriage saying in the creation account. The Christ-and-Church interpretation in the next Ephesians unit is not silently written into Genesis itself.

The explicit Christ-and-Church reference relates to the earlier identification of the Church as His body. The current argument follows the marriage/one-flesh saying; the earlier body/fullness unit does not use the same mystery or marriage formulation.

Both give paired instructions to wives and husbands. Ephesians says husbandly self-like love and wifely respect; Colossians says wives submit as fitting in the Lord and husbands love without bitterness. Respect and submission are not made identical printed terms.

Both command children to obey their parents. Colossians adds in everything and says this pleases in the Lord; Ephesians says in the Lord and because it is right. The qualifications and stated grounds remain distinct.

The honor-father-and-mother command corresponds to Exodus's command and its promised well-being and long life. Ephesians additionally calls it the first command with a promise; that description is not another sentence of Exodus20:12.

The well-being/long-life promise corresponds to the parental-honor command's promise in Deuteronomy. Ephesians says upon the earth; Deuteronomy's full land-and-divine-gift wording is retained in the target rather than imported into the shorter citation.

Both tell fathers not to provoke their children. Ephesians positively names nourishment in the Lord's discipline and admonition; Colossians names the risk that the children lose heart. The different grounds and responses are kept distinct.

Both instruct slaves regarding fleshly masters and sincere hearts in relation to the Lord. Ephesians also names fear and trembling and service as to Christ; Colossians names the fear of the Lord and rejects people-pleasing.

Both reject eye-service and people-pleasing in the slaves' instructions. Ephesians additionally names being Christ's slaves and doing God's will from the soul; Colossians names sincere hearts and fearing the Lord. The grounds remain distinct.
Both direct service or work toward the Lord rather than people. Ephesians names goodwill; Colossians names work from the soul in whatever is done. Their particular descriptors remain as printed.

Both connect work with receiving from the Lord. Ephesians names whatever good is done and slave/free alike; Colossians names inheritance's recompense and also the wrongdoer's return without partiality. Good and wrongdoing are not made the same stated condition.

Both address masters in light of their own Master in heaven. Ephesians requires giving up threats and names divine impartiality; Colossians requires what is right and equitable for slaves. The different duties are retained rather than equated.

Both describe empowerment through divine might. Colossians describes being empowered according to the might of His glory for endurance and patience; Ephesians commands strength in the Lord and His might. The command and participial description retain their different forms.

Both use putting on armament for Christian conduct. Romans names light's weapons against works of darkness; Ephesians names God's full armor to stand against the devil's schemes. The tactical images and surrounding instructions differ.

Both name rulers and authorities in accounts of conflict or triumph. Colossians describes their being stripped and publicly led in triumph; Ephesians explicitly identifies its opponents as spiritual forces rather than flesh and blood. The comparison does not settle the precise identity of every ruler in Colossians.

Taking up the full armor and standing in the evil day resumes the earlier command to put on God's full armor to stand against the devil's schemes. This is an internal instruction and development, not a separately reconstructed battle.

Truth fastened around the waist relates to Isaiah's righteousness and truth as girding around the waist and sides. The named clothing qualities and figures remain distinct; the breastplate component is not claimed to appear in this Isaiah unit.

The breastplate of righteousness has a specific counterpart in Isaiah's divine-warrior armor. Isaiah also names salvation's helmet and a garment of vengeance; those components are not all inserted into Ephesians's particular breastplate clause. The supplied Isaiah unit ends with the cloak, without an added zeal description.

Feet made ready with the gospel of peace relate to Isaiah's feet of a good-news proclaimer and report of peace. Isaiah describes a messenger and God's reign in Zion; Ephesians uses footwear in its armor image. The wording is not an identical quotation.

Both connect resisting the devil with faith. Peter's letter uses the prowling-lion image and firmness in faith; Ephesians uses faith's shield extinguishing the evil one's flaming arrows. The animal and warfare images are not merged into one literal attack.

The helmet of salvation corresponds to Isaiah's salvation helmet in the divine-warrior description. Ephesians also names the Spirit's sword as God's word; Isaiah59:17 does not supply that whole sword clause.

Praying at every time corresponds to the instruction to pray without ceasing. Ephesians also names prayer in the Spirit, watchfulness, perseverance and all saints. The shorter Thessalonian command is not expanded as though it printed every one of those details.

Both request prayer for speaking a mystery. Ephesians asks for a word and boldness when opening the mouth to make known the gospel's mystery; Colossians asks for a door for the word to speak Christ's mystery and names bonds. The requests and opening images remain distinct.

Both use ambassador language for service on Christ's behalf. Corinthians describes God's appeal for reconciliation through the speakers; Ephesians names a chained ambassador asking for bold speech. The chain is not supplied as a fact in the selected Corinthians unit.

Both name Tychicus as the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord who reports the writer's circumstances. Colossians also calls him a fellow slave. The repeated named role does not by itself establish an identical delivery date.

Both describe the purpose of sending the messenger as making circumstances known and encouraging the recipients' hearts. The actual directions of knowing and the pronouns are preserved, without inventing a second personal name for the messenger.

The closing peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ corresponds to the opening grace-and-peace greeting from the same named divine persons. The closing adds love with faith and addresses brothers; the opening's grace is not silently inserted here.

Both close with grace directed to the recipients in relation to the Lord Jesus. Ephesians addresses all who love Him in incorruptibility; Corinthians gives the short grace blessing. Incorruptibility is retained without replacing it with an unprinted sincerity formula.
